Worked example: North Carolina

Justin Chase

Source: vignettes/spatialkit_nc_demo.Rmd
spatialkit_nc_demo.Rmd

This article runs the pipeline on a simulated field over North Carolina, where the structure the cells and models should find is known, and compares four tessellations, two fold schemes and two backends on it. vignette("getting-started") takes the short path through the same steps. The state outline comes from the nc.shp file bundled with sf, so the article needs no other files.

This article needs six optional packages: ggplot2 for the figures, patchwork for the stacked panels, geometry for the Delaunay triangles, ranger for the random forest, sp for GWR and gstat for the variogram. Where one is missing, the code that needs it is shown but not run.

The state outline, in feet 

library(spatialkit)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)

The chunk below dissolves the county boundaries shipped with sf into one state outline and projects it to NAD83 / North Carolina (ftUS), EPSG:2264, so that distances are planar. Every distance and block size below is therefore in US survey feet, not metres (the GWR bandwidth is a count of neighbours). Projected does not mean metric: the unit is the one the CRS names.

nc_counties <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
nc_boundary <- nc_counties |>
  st_union() |>
  st_transform(2264) |>
  st_as_sf()

A simulated field with known structure

Three hundred points inside the outline carry two predictors and a response:

  • elevation rises from west to east, plus noise.
  • pop_density decays with the distance from two invented cities.
  • y is the sum of the two predictors’ effects, a spatial field that neither predictor carries, and noise. The field is structure that nearby observations share, so a model’s error depends on how far from the data it predicts.
n_points <- 300

pts_raw    <- st_sample(nc_boundary, size = n_points, type = "random")
pts_coords <- st_coordinates(pts_raw)
x_coords   <- pts_coords[, 1]
y_coords   <- pts_coords[, 2]

elevation <- scale(x_coords)[, 1] * 500 + rnorm(n_points, 3000, 400)

city1 <- c(1530000, 550000)   # near Charlotte in EPSG:2264
city2 <- c(2150000, 750000)   # near Raleigh
dist_to_city <- pmin(
  sqrt((x_coords - city1[1])^2 + (y_coords - city1[2])^2),
  sqrt((x_coords - city2[1])^2 + (y_coords - city2[2])^2)
)
pop_density <- pmax(exp(-dist_to_city / 400000) * 5000 + rnorm(n_points, 200, 100), 10)

spatial_field <- 20 * sin(x_coords / 250000) * cos(y_coords / 250000)

y_response <- 50 +
  0.01  * elevation +
  0.005 * pop_density +
  spatial_field +
  rnorm(n_points, 0, 5)

points_sf <- st_sf(
  y           = y_response,
  elevation   = elevation,
  pop_density = pop_density,
  geometry    = pts_raw
)
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = nc_boundary, fill = "grey95", colour = "black") +
  geom_sf(data = points_sf, aes(colour = y), size = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "Response (y)") +
  theme_void() +
  ggtitle("Simulated observations")

Four tessellations

build_tessellation() builds four kinds of cell from the same points and outline; vignette("cells") says which kind suits which purpose. The counts are set by hand, 40 seeds for the Voronoi cells and about 50 cells for each grid, so that the methods are compared at similar numbers of cells. vignette("resolution") shows how to choose the count from the data.

Voronoi cells from 40 density-weighted k-means seeds

Voronoi cells grow around seed points, not around the observations. One cell per observation would give 300 cells of one point each: a nearest-neighbour interpolation rather than an aggregation, with no spread inside a cell to compute a standard error from. get_voronoi_seeds() clusters the observations first, each weighted by its local density, so cells are small where the observations are dense.

seeds <- get_voronoi_seeds(
  boundary      = nc_boundary,
  sample_points = points_sf,
  method        = "kmeans",
  n             = 40
)

tess_voronoi <- build_tessellation(
  seeds, boundary = nc_boundary,
  method = "voronoi", clip = TRUE, quiet = TRUE
)
outside <- lengths(st_intersects(seeds, nc_boundary)) == 0
sum(outside)                   # seeds that lie outside the state outline
## [1] 1
tess_voronoi$index[outside]    # the cell each of them generates
## [1] 38

A k-means centre is a mean of observations, so it can lie outside an outline that is not convex. Here 1 of the 40 centres lies just outside the state outline, over a sound that coastal observations surround. Its cell, the part of the state nearer to it than to any other seed, is still built inside the outline. For seeds, tess_voronoi$index holds the cell_id each seed generates, including this one.

Hex and square grids of about 50 cells 

tess_hex <- build_tessellation(
  points_sf, boundary = nc_boundary,
  method = "hex", approx_n_cells = 50, clip = TRUE, quiet = TRUE
)

tess_square <- build_tessellation(
  points_sf, boundary = nc_boundary,
  method = "square", approx_n_cells = 50, clip = TRUE, quiet = TRUE
)

All four methods return cells with a cell_id column; the grid methods keep poly_id beside it, holding the same values.

names(tess_hex$cells)
## [1] "poly_id"  "geometry" "cell_id"

Delaunay triangles

method = "triangles" uses geometry::delaunayn() when geometry is installed, and otherwise falls back to sf::st_triangulate() with a logged warning. Both give the Delaunay triangulation of the points; they can split degenerate (co-circular) configurations differently.

tess_tri <- build_tessellation(
  points_sf, boundary = nc_boundary,
  method = "triangles", clip = TRUE, quiet = TRUE
)
tri_assigned <- assign_features_to_polygons(points_sf, tess_tri$cells,
                                            polygon_id_col = "cell_id")
c(triangles   = nrow(tess_tri$cells),
  with_points = length(unique(na.omit(tri_assigned$cell_id))))
##   triangles with_points 
##         586         189

The corners of the triangles are the observations themselves, so each observation falls in one of the triangles that meet at it, and most triangles hold none: 189 of 586 hold a point here. ?build_tessellation describes triangles as useful for interpolation and adjacency work, not as an aggregation unit.

The number of cells each method built:

sapply(list(Voronoi = tess_voronoi, Hex = tess_hex, Square = tess_square,
            Triangles = tess_tri),
       function(tess) nrow(tess$cells))
##   Voronoi       Hex    Square Triangles 
##        40        49        45       586

Cell means and their standard errors

assign_features_to_polygons() puts each point in a cell, and summarize_by_cell() reduces the points to one row per cell. Each row holds the count n; the mean, standard deviation and standard error of the response and of every predictor; a cell_weight; and beside each mean a pooled value, the cell’s mean pulled toward the mean of the observations in the 8 nearest cells (nearest by the centroid of their observations). vignette("cells") explains pooled values and when to report one.

assigned <- assign_features_to_polygons(points_sf, tess_voronoi$cells,
                                        polygon_id_col = "cell_id")

cell_stats <- summarize_by_cell(
  assigned,
  response_var   = "y",
  predictor_vars = c("elevation", "pop_density"),
  id_col         = "cell_id"
)

head(as.data.frame(cell_stats)[, c("cell_id", "n", "resp_mean_y", "..se_resp_y",
                                   "..pooled_resp_y")])
##   cell_id n resp_mean_y ..se_resp_y ..pooled_resp_y
## 1       1 6    62.89141    2.888004        65.90426
## 2       2 7    63.36230    2.840840        66.32647
## 3       3 5    67.11282    3.810849        69.71523
## 4       4 5    70.34951    5.557886        72.31561
## 5       5 5    79.61205    2.382507        80.23328
## 6       6 4    84.14516    3.943018        84.77772

The ..se_* columns are standard errors at the default deff = 1, which treats the points in a cell as independent. That is the standard error of each cell’s own mean, the value a map of the cells shows, when the points are spread through the cell. As a standard error for the population mean it is anticonservative when points inside a cell are spatially correlated, and deff = "kish" widens it by a design effect estimated from that correlation; vignette("cells") explains the design effect.

cell_kish <- summarize_by_cell(
  assigned,
  response_var   = "y",
  predictor_vars = c("elevation", "pop_density"),
  id_col         = "cell_id",
  deff           = "kish"
)

deff <- attr(cell_kish, "deff_applied")
cat(sprintf("method = %s | ICC(response) = %.3f | median design effect = %.2f\n",
            deff$method, deff$icc_resp, stats::median(deff$deff, na.rm = TRUE)))
## method = kish | ICC(response) = 0.737 | median design effect = 5.42
# How much the Kish standard error of the response exceeds the default one.
inflation <- cell_kish$`..se_resp_y` / cell_stats$`..se_resp_y`
summary(inflation)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   3.067   4.220   4.540   4.624   5.120   6.973

The Kish standard error is a median 4.54 times the default one, more than the 2.33 that the square root of the median design effect gives, because an estimated design effect also corrects the within-cell standard deviation (vignette("cells"), “Standard errors and the design effect”).

Maps of the cell means

summarize_by_cell(cells_sf = ) returns the summary on the cells themselves, ready for plot_tessellation_map(). The two helpers below summarise a tessellation onto its cells and map the mean of y:

# The cell summary of y on the cells of one tessellation.
on_cells <- function(tess) {
  assigned <- assign_features_to_polygons(points_sf, tess$cells,
                                          polygon_id_col = "cell_id")
  summarize_by_cell(assigned, response_var = "y", id_col = "cell_id",
                    cells_sf = tess$cells)
}

# A map of the cell means, on a colour scale with the given limits.
map_means <- function(cells, label, limits = NULL) {
  plot_tessellation_map(
    tessellation_sf = cells,
    boundary        = nc_boundary,
    fill_col        = "resp_mean_y",
    outline_col     = "white",
    outline_size    = 0.3,
    boundary_col    = "grey20",
    boundary_size   = 0.8,
    title           = sprintf("%s, %d cells", label, nrow(cells))
  ) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Mean y", limits = limits, na.value = "grey60")
}

The three maps below share one colour scale: its limits span all three sets of cell means, and patchwork collects the three legends into one, so a colour means the same value on every map. Grey cells hold no observation.

library(patchwork)

means <- lapply(list(Voronoi = tess_voronoi, Hex = tess_hex, Square = tess_square),
                on_cells)
lims  <- range(unlist(lapply(means, `[[`, "resp_mean_y")), na.rm = TRUE)

(map_means(means$Voronoi, "Voronoi", lims) /
 map_means(means$Hex,     "Hex",     lims) /
 map_means(means$Square,  "Square",  lims)) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")

The triangle map, on its own colour scale:

map_means(on_cells(tess_tri), "Delaunay triangles")

Models fitted on the points

The models below are fitted on the 300 points, not on the cell means; vignette("getting-started") says when to fit on cells instead. The cells can still serve as cross-validation blocks: make_folds(points_sf, k = 5, method = "block_kfold", blocks = tess_voronoi$cells) holds out whole Voronoi cells.

A random forest and its residuals

fit_rf_model() and cv_rf() need ranger.

rf_fit <- fit_rf_model(points_sf, response_var = "y",
                       predictor_vars = c("elevation", "pop_density"))
rf_fit
## <Random Forest (ranger)> spatial model fit
##   Formula : y ~ elevation + pop_density
##   n       : 300
##   CRS     : EPSG:2264
##   Trees   : 500 (mtry = 1, min node = 5)
##   Coords as predictors: no - no spatial information used; see ?fit_rf_model
##   Sampling: bootstrap, with replacement (100.0% of rows per tree)
##   OOB RMSE: 9.7284   OOB R^2: 0.4733
##   Importance (permutation): elevation=105.4, pop_density=83.25
## 
##   OOB is a random hold-out: under spatial autocorrelation it is the error
##   of predicting among the samples, and reads low for predictions made
##   farther from the data than the samples sit from each other. Score a map
##   that predicts farther with cv_rf() on folds at its distances
##   (?fold_separation).

summary.spatial_fit() on an rf_fit reports out-of-bag metrics, not in-sample ones: fitted.rf_fit() returns out-of-bag predictions, and the printout says so. A gwr_fit or bayesian_fit reports in-sample metrics, so the two are not comparable; scores from the same folds are, as the comparison of backends below shows.

summary(rf_fit)
## Summary of <rf_fit> fit (n = 300)
## 
##   Formula: y ~ elevation + pop_density
## 
##   Out-of-bag metrics (NOT in-sample; see ?fit_rf_model):
##     RMSE    = 9.7284
##     MAE     = 7.8448
##     R^2     = 0.4715
##     SMAPE   = 8.65%
rf_fit$info$importance     # coef() on an rf_fit errors: a forest has no coefficients
##   elevation pop_density 
##   105.35583    83.25089

The two printouts give different R² (0.4733 above, 0.4715 here) and the same RMSE. Both read the same out-of-bag predictions. print.rf_fit() echoes the R² that ranger reports, which compares the out-of-bag mean squared error with the variance of y computed with denominator n − 1; summary.spatial_fit() uses denominator n. Their unexplained fractions therefore differ by the factor n / (n − 1), here 300 / 299.

plot.spatial_fit() draws the residuals on a map by default (type = "residuals"); "observed_predicted", "variogram" and, for a GWR fit, "coefficients" are the other views. Structure in the residual map is spatial autocorrelation the model has not captured, and residual_morans_i() puts a number on it.

plot(rf_fit, type = "residuals")

mi <- residual_morans_i(rf_fit)
cat(sprintf("Moran's I = %.4f (z = %.2f, p = %.3g)\n",
            mi$observed, mi$z, mi$p_value))
## Moran's I = 0.5443 (z = 20.12, p = 4.58e-90)

The residuals are autocorrelated (Moran’s I = 0.54, z = 20.1): the forest has not captured the spatial field added to y, which neither predictor carries. The section on spatial folds measures what that does to a cross-validated score.

A GWR fit, if sp is installed 

gwr_fit <- fit_gwr_model(
  data_sf        = points_sf,
  response_var   = "y",
  predictor_vars = c("elevation", "pop_density"),
  adaptive       = TRUE,
  kernel         = "bisquare"
)

gwr_met <- model_metrics(gwr_fit)
# adaptive = TRUE: the bandwidth is a number of nearest neighbours, not feet.
cat(sprintf("Bandwidth: %.0f neighbours | in-sample R2: %.3f | RMSE: %.3f\n",
            gwr_fit$info$bandwidth, gwr_met$R2, gwr_met$RMSE))
## Bandwidth: 44 neighbours | in-sample R2: 0.877 | RMSE: 4.701

GWR fits one weighted regression at each location, so each coefficient has a value at every point. type = "coefficients" maps one of them:

plot(gwr_fit, type = "coefficients", term = "elevation")

The simulation gives elevation the same effect, 0.01, everywhere, so the spread on the map is not variation in the true effect.

In 25 of the 300 windows the local intercept is poorly determined: the condition index that includes the intercept (cn in gwr_fit$info$local_collinearity, see ?fit_gwr_model) is above 30. The cause is elevation, which averages about 3,000 but inside a window of 44 neighbours varies by little more than the noise the simulation added (standard deviation 400), so locally it is nearly collinear with the intercept. The slopes are well determined: their index (cn_slopes), which centres the predictors in each window, is at most 4.5, so the fit does not warn, and the elevation map above masks no location. With term = "Intercept" the same map draws the poorly determined intercepts hollow. Centring the predictor (elevation - mean(elevation)) gives the same bandwidth and fitted values and determines the intercepts too.

Scoring the model on spatial folds

A random fold leaves each held-out point’s neighbours in the training data; a blocked fold holds out whole blocks of the state. With residuals as autocorrelated as the forest’s, the two schemes can give different scores; the runs below measure the difference on these data.

The autocorrelation range

estimate_sac_range() fits a variogram to the residuals of y on the predictors and returns the autocorrelation range of the residuals in CRS units, here US survey feet. It returns NA when the variogram never levels off within the distances it was fitted over, because a range it cannot identify must not size the blocks. ?estimate_sac_range covers the directional fits and anisotropy.

sac <- estimate_sac_range(points_sf, response_var = "y",
                          predictor_vars = c("elevation", "pop_density"))
as.numeric(sac)
## [1] NA
attr(sac, "rejected_reason")
## [1] "fitted range exceeds the largest lag fitted"

plot.sac_range() draws the empirical variogram with the fitted model, so you can judge the fit; when no range was identified, the subtitle says why. Here the fitted curve is still rising at the largest distance it was fitted over.

plot(sac)

Random folds and blocks

No range was identified, so the block size here comes from the simulation instead. The field changes sign about every 785,000 ft (π × 250,000), and 400,000 ft is about half that, the distance from a zero of the wave to its peak. On your own data, where the field is unknown, cv_block_size_sweep() gives the cross-validated error at each block size (vignette("spatial-cross-validation")).

folds_random  <- make_folds(points_sf, k = 5, method = "random_kfold", seed = 42)
folds_blocked <- make_folds(points_sf, k = 5, method = "block_kfold",
                            block_size = 400000, seed = 42)

c(random = folds_random$k, blocked = folds_blocked$k,
  blocks = folds_blocked$params$blocks_used)
##  random blocked  blocks 
##       5       5      12

plot_folds() shows whether the blocks separate the data, and how wide they are:

library(patchwork)
(plot_folds(folds_random,  points_sf, boundary = nc_boundary) /
 plot_folds(folds_blocked, points_sf, boundary = nc_boundary)) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")

The score under each scheme

include_coords = TRUE gives the forest the coordinates, which lets it fit the training surface by location, so its error grows quickly with the distance from the data. Scoring it with the same predictors and settings on both fold schemes shows how much:

cv_random  <- cv_rf(points_sf, "y", c("elevation", "pop_density"),
                    folds = folds_random, include_coords = TRUE,
                    num_trees = 300, seed = 1)
cv_blocked <- cv_rf(points_sf, "y", c("elevation", "pop_density"),
                    folds = folds_blocked, include_coords = TRUE,
                    num_trees = 300, seed = 1)

data.frame(
  folds = c("random_kfold", "block_kfold"),
  R2    = c(cv_random$overall$R2,   cv_blocked$overall$R2),
  RMSE  = c(cv_random$overall$RMSE, cv_blocked$overall$RMSE)
)
##          folds        R2     RMSE
## 1 random_kfold 0.7945102 6.090085
## 2  block_kfold 0.6313066 8.994703

Random folds report R² = 0.795; blocked folds report 0.631 with the same predictors and settings, a drop of 21 percent of the reported skill.

Which of the two to report depends on where the map will predict. The random score is the error of predicting among the points you have; the blocked one is the error of predicting whole blocks of the state from the rest. The surface mapped at the end of this article covers the state these points were sampled across at random. fold_separation() compares the distances from such a map’s locations to the data with the held-out distances of each scheme. Here map_pts, a regular sample of the state, stands in for that map’s grid:

map_pts <- st_sample(nc_boundary, size = 2000, type = "regular")
reading <- c(
  random  = attr(fold_separation(folds_random,  points_sf,
                                 prediction_points = map_pts), "target")$reading,
  blocked = attr(fold_separation(folds_blocked, points_sf,
                                 prediction_points = map_pts), "target")$reading)
reading
##    random   blocked 
## "matched" "farther"

"matched" says the held-out points sit about as far from their training data as the map’s locations sit from the data; "farther" says they sit farther, so that score tends to read high for this map. The reading compares nearest-neighbour distances and does not measure a bias. ?fold_separation lists all four readings, and vignette("spatial-cross-validation") explains them. For a map of an area the points never sampled, the blocked score would be the closer match.

The comparison of backends below and the area of applicability of the surface use the random folds, the scheme fold_separation() reads as matched for this map.

Two backends on the same folds

compare_models_cv() cross-validates each requested backend on the folds you pass, so their scores are comparable. A backend whose package is missing is dropped with a message, and the call returns the backends that could run.

cmp <- compare_models_cv(
  points_sf, "y", c("elevation", "pop_density"),
  models   = c("RF", "GWR"),
  folds    = folds_random,
  rf_args  = list(num_trees = 300)
)
cmp$overall[, c("model", "RMSE", "MAE", "R2")]
##   model     RMSE      MAE        R2
## 1   GWR 5.591604 4.454352 0.8267726
## 2    RF 9.823995 7.859748 0.4652879

The RF row is the forest on the two predictors alone; on the same random folds the forest with coordinates scored R² = 0.795. The field is a smooth wave that neither predictor carries, and a forest given the coordinates can fit it by location.

A surface, and where it applies

predict_surface() builds a regular grid over the training extent, takes each grid point’s covariates from the nearest observation, clips the grid to the outline and predicts. The map below uses rf_fit, the forest on the two predictors alone.

surf <- predict_surface(rf_fit, n_cells = 3000,
                        covariates = points_sf, boundary = nc_boundary)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = surf, aes(colour = .pred), size = 0.6) +
  geom_sf(data = nc_boundary, fill = NA, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "Predicted y") +
  theme_void() +
  ggtitle("Predicted surface")

A fitted model returns a number for any location you hand it, including locations whose predictor values look nothing like the training data. area_of_applicability() marks where the cross-validated score applies. Pass it the folds the score came from, here the random ones:

aoa <- area_of_applicability(surf, model = rf_fit, folds = folds_random)

cat(sprintf("inside: %d | outside: %d | undetermined: %d | DI threshold %.3f\n",
            aoa$n_inside, aoa$n_outside, aoa$n_na, aoa$threshold))
## inside: 1645 | outside: 0 | undetermined: 0 | DI threshold 0.152
# To blank the map outside the area. AOA is NA where a predictor is missing;
# count those as outside.
surf$.pred_masked <- ifelse(aoa$aoa$AOA %in% TRUE, surf$.pred, NA_real_)

No grid point is outside, because predict_surface(covariates = points_sf) copies predictor values from the nearest observation: every grid point carries a predictor vector some training point already had, so its dissimilarity index is 0 by construction. The index is useful when the covariates come from elsewhere, such as a raster, a different survey or a future scenario. Given values outside the training range, it marks them:

extreme <- st_sf(
  elevation   = c(mean(points_sf$elevation), max(points_sf$elevation) * 4),
  pop_density = c(mean(points_sf$pop_density), max(points_sf$pop_density) * 4),
  geometry    = st_geometry(points_sf)[1:2]
)
st_drop_geometry(area_of_applicability(extreme, model = rf_fit,
                                       folds = folds_random)$aoa)[, c("DI", "AOA")]
##            DI   AOA
## 1  0.04806484  TRUE
## 2 15.68668080 FALSE

Next

vignette("troubleshooting") lists the errors and warnings you are most likely to meet, what each means, and how to handle large layers, parallel folds, caches and the log. The main help pages this article relies on are ?build_tessellation, ?summarize_by_cell, ?fit_rf_model, ?fit_gwr_model, ?estimate_sac_range, ?make_folds, ?fold_separation, ?compare_models_cv and ?area_of_applicability, and vignette("glossary") defines the terms. The script system.file("scripts", "example_nc_demo.R", package = "spatialkit") runs this example’s steps as one script at the console and writes its figures to a temporary folder.
